paragraphs: A symmetry describes a transformation that preserves relevant properties of data. Models can benefit from knowing these transformations, but that knowledge is often supplied in advance. This paper develops a generative model that learns approximate symmetries from data, extending a line of research that has largely focused on discriminative models.

The method starts with a broad, prespecified collection of possible transformations. It then learns how strongly those transformations are supported by the dataset, including whether a proposed symmetry is present at all. Drawing on ideas from group theory, the model represents transformations as part of a generative process. This also gives it an interpretation as a learned mechanism for data augmentation.

The authors provide a simple learning algorithm and demonstrate interpretable recovery of symmetries involving affine and color transformations. When combined with standard generative models, their symmetry model improves marginal test log-likelihood and data efficiency in the reported experiments. The contribution is therefore a way to learn the extent of candidate symmetries, with demonstrated benefits for generative modeling.
neurips-2024-a-generative-model-of-symme.tldr: A generative model learns how much candidate symmetry transformations apply to a dataset, improving generative modeling and data efficiency in experiments.

paragraphs: Medical image models can struggle when images come from a different hospital or when demographic variables are entangled with prediction targets. This paper studies these domain shifts in chest X-rays and skin lesion images. Its empirical finding is that existing visual backbones lack an architectural prior appropriate for reliable generalization in the settings examined.

The proposed Knowledge-enhanced Bottlenecks, or KnoBo, constrain predictions to pass through clinically relevant concepts. These concepts come from explicit medical knowledge expressed in natural language, such as material in textbooks or PubMed. Retrieval-augmented language models help design the concept space, while an automatic training procedure teaches the system to recognize those concepts in images.

The evaluation spans 20 datasets and two imaging modalities, comparing knowledge resources and recognition architectures across domain shifts. On confounded datasets, KnoBo outperforms fine-tuned models by a reported average of 32.4%. PubMed performs particularly well in information diversity and final prediction performance. These findings support using explicit medical concepts to reduce sensitivity to the evaluated shifts.
neurips-2024-a-textbook-remedy-for-domai.tldr: KnoBo uses medical knowledge to constrain image predictions through clinical concepts, improving performance under evaluated domain shifts.

paragraphs: Aligner addresses the practical difficulty of updating language model behavior as requirements change. Its central idea is to train a smaller model to correct responses produced by an upstream model. Training focuses on the changes that separate dispreferred answers from preferred ones, making correction a reusable capability.

The resulting module is designed to work across open-source and API-based models after a single training process. The paper also describes an iterative use: corrected responses become synthetic preference data for further improving the upstream model. This connects correction at deployment with a possible training loop, allowing the same correction mechanism to support both immediate response improvements and subsequent model updates.

Experiments apply the same Aligner to 11 language models and evaluate helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty. Aligner-7B delivers reported average improvements of 68.9% in helpfulness and 22.8% in harmlessness, while reducing hallucination. These results support the usefulness of a shared correction model across the tested systems, rather than requiring a separately trained corrector for every upstream model.
neurips-2024-aligner-efficient-alignment.tldr: Aligner trains a reusable smaller model to correct language model responses, improving alignment measures across 11 tested models.

paragraphs: Turning a natural-language question into SQL requires understanding what the user means. Some questions support multiple interpretations, even when the relevant database is available. AMBROSIA is a benchmark designed to test whether text-to-SQL systems can recognize and interpret this ambiguity, rather than treating every question as having one clear meaning.

The dataset covers scope ambiguity, attachment ambiguity, and vagueness. Each question is accompanied by its interpretations and corresponding SQL queries, so the benchmark represents the different executable meanings a request can have. The authors construct databases from scratch through a controlled generation process. This ensures that database context does not resolve the ambiguity that the question is intended to test.

Evaluations of several language models show that even the most advanced models tested struggle to identify and interpret ambiguous questions. The result highlights a specific weakness in translating user requests into database operations. AMBROSIA supplies a focused resource for studying that weakness and developing parsers that account for multiple plausible readings.
neurips-2024-ambrosia-a-benchmark-for-pa.tldr: AMBROSIA tests ambiguity in text-to-SQL requests and finds that advanced language models struggle even when database context is available.

paragraphs: A prediction-assisted search algorithm can use a guess about where a target lies in a sorted array. This paper asks what changes when the prediction is a probability distribution over targets. That setting preserves uncertainty in the prediction, which a single guessed position cannot fully express.

The authors show that some simple distributions make the classical point-prediction approach perform poorly regardless of which single prediction it uses. They develop an algorithm with query complexity O(H(p) + log η), where H(p) is the entropy of the true target distribution and η is the earth mover's distance between the true and predicted distributions. The bound connects search cost to both uncertainty about the target and distributional prediction error.

The result also yields a distributionally robust algorithm for constructing an optimal binary search tree from a target distribution. A lower bound establishes essential optimality up to constants, and experiments support practical usefulness. Together, these findings show why the distribution itself can be valuable algorithmic input.
neurips-2024-binary-search-with-distribu.tldr: A search algorithm uses full predicted distributions and achieves essentially optimal query complexity tied to target uncertainty and prediction error.

paragraphs: Understanding a video involves tracking relationships among objects as those relationships change over time. This paper introduces AeroEye, a dataset for studying these relationships in drone footage. It contains varied aerial scenes and relationship labels that describe both interactions and spatial arrangements among objects.

The proposed Cyclic Graph Transformer, or CYCLO, maintains a history of interactions through circular updates. This mechanism is intended to capture immediate connections as well as dependencies across more distant moments. It also preserves the sequential order of object relationships while accommodating recurring patterns. That combination matters for periodic or overlapping relationships, where useful history needs to remain available as the sequence progresses.

Experiments on AeroEye demonstrate the method's effectiveness and support its potential for understanding drone videos. CYCLO also consistently achieves state-of-the-art results on the PVSG and ASPIRe scene graph benchmarks. The paper therefore contributes both a dataset focused on aerial relationships and a temporal modeling approach evaluated on that dataset and two additional benchmarks.
neurips-2024-cyclo-cyclic-graph-transfor.tldr: CYCLO uses circular interaction-history updates to model video relationships, alongside the new AeroEye dataset for aerial scenes.

paragraphs: Real-world data analysis often asks for useful reasoning about an application, beyond retrieving a fact or performing arithmetic. DACO builds resources for this broader task, which combines mathematical, logical, and strategic reasoning. The authors use language models supported by code generation to create analyses, with human refinement supplying a concentrated, higher-quality evaluation set.

The dataset contains 440 real-world tabular databases and approximately 2,000 automatically generated query-answer pairs. These pairs provide weak supervision: training material produced automatically rather than entirely through expert annotation. The human-refined test set serves a different role, providing the main benchmark for assessing how helpful an analysis is.

In the evaluation, outputs from models such as GPT-4 are judged less helpful than human-written analyses in 58.1% of cases. Training with DACO's weak supervision produces a model that outperforms existing table-question-answering baselines. Reinforcement learning from human feedback further improves helpfulness in 58.5% of cases. The findings support combining scalable generated training data with human-informed evaluation and refinement.
neurips-2024-daco-towards-application-dr.tldr: DACO supplies data and evaluation for application-driven analysis, showing benefits from generated supervision and human-feedback training.

paragraphs: DeTrack treats visual object tracking as a process of removing noise from a bounding box. During training, the method perturbs boxes to create noisy examples, using denoising learning to improve robustness on unseen data. This offers a different way to learn box prediction from image-feature regression or coordinate autoregression.

Repeatedly running a diffusion model would impose a substantial speed cost on tracking. DeTrack instead distributes denoising across blocks within a single Vision Transformer. Each block receives template and search embeddings as conditions and removes some noise from the box prediction. The stacked blocks cooperate to complete the denoising process within the model.

The tracker then uses image features and trajectory information to refine the resulting box. Visual memory and trajectory memory also support tracking stability. Experiments report competitive performance on several challenging datasets while maintaining real-time speed. The central finding is that placing denoising stages inside the architecture can make this learning approach practical for the time constraints of visual tracking.
neurips-2024-detrack-in-model-latent-den.tldr: DeTrack denoises bounding boxes through internal Transformer blocks, achieving competitive tracking performance at real-time speed.

paragraphs: Non-autoregressive Transformers generate images by progressively revealing latent image tokens. At each step, the model predicts masked regions and retains its most reliable predictions. This paper examines which interactions make that process work and which computations are largely repeated without substantially changing token representations.

Within a generation step, the authors find an asymmetry: masked tokens mainly gather information, while visible tokens mainly supply it. Across steps, updates concentrate on a few critical tokens, with much of the remaining computation repeated. EfficientNAT, or ENAT, builds these observations into its architecture. It encodes visible tokens independently, then decodes masked tokens using the encoded visible information.

ENAT also concentrates each step's computation on critical tokens and reuses previously computed representations to provide other necessary information. Experiments on ImageNet at two resolutions and on MS-COCO report improved performance with significantly lower computational cost. The results support organizing computation around the different roles of tokens and the limited changes needed between generation steps.
neurips-2024-enat-rethinking-spatial-tem.tldr: ENAT improves token-based image generation efficiency by separating token roles and reusing representations across generation steps.

paragraphs: Guidance lets a pretrained diffusion model steer its outputs toward a user-specified objective. This paper develops a mathematical framework for understanding gradient guidance as optimization. Its analysis connects guided sampling to a regularized optimization problem, with the pretraining data supplying the regularization that shapes which solutions are generated.

Simply inserting the gradient of an external objective can damage structure in the generated samples. The authors instead investigate guidance based on a forward prediction loss. This form uses information from pretrained score functions and comes with a proof of latent-structure preservation. The design therefore connects the desired objective with information already captured by the diffusion model.

The paper also studies an iterative procedure that updates both guidance and the score network using newly generated samples. In expectation, this procedure behaves like a first-order optimization iteration. For concave objectives, the authors prove convergence to the global optimum at a rate of approximately 1/K, up to logarithmic factors. That global guarantee is tied to the stated concavity condition.
neurips-2024-gradient-guidance-for-diffu.tldr: An optimization framework explains gradient-guided diffusion and provides structure-preserving guidance with a conditional global convergence guarantee.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often use normalization layers originally developed for other kinds of data. The paper argues that these layers may miss properties of graph structure and can potentially weaken a model's expressive power. Existing graph-specific alternatives also do not consistently deliver substantial benefits, motivating a normalization rule that adapts more directly to each graph.

GRANOLA normalizes node features using representations tailored to the graph being processed. It constructs these representations by propagating random node features through the graph. Those propagated features supply expressive information about nodes, allowing normalization to respond to the graph's characteristics rather than applying an unadapted rule.

The authors provide theoretical support for their design and an extensive empirical comparison with existing normalization techniques. GRANOLA performs better in that evaluation and is the top-performing method among the compared baselines in the same time-complexity class as message-passing neural networks. The findings indicate that normalization itself can be a useful place to incorporate graph-dependent information.
neurips-2024-granola-adaptive-normalizat.tldr: GRANOLA adapts graph-network normalization using propagated random node features, improving performance over evaluated normalization methods.

paragraphs: Language models commonly learn by maximizing the likelihood of the next token in training examples. This paper explores a broader imitation-learning approach: inverse reinforcement learning, which extracts rewards and optimizes sequences. The aim is to use the sequential structure of language generation more directly during supervised fine-tuning.

The authors reformulate inverse soft-Q-learning as maximum likelihood estimation extended with temporal-difference regularization. This establishes a principled connection between the familiar token-prediction objective and inverse reinforcement learning. It also provides a way to balance added training complexity against improvements in task performance and generation diversity.

The reported findings favor inverse-reinforcement-learning-based imitation, particularly when preserving diverse outputs while maximizing task performance. These benefits appear with fixed supervised fine-tuning datasets, without requiring online data generation. Analysis of the extracted reward functions also indicates potential benefits for reward robustness when supervised and preference-based post-training are more tightly integrated. The contribution combines an alternative training perspective with a formulation connected to standard language model learning.
neurips-2024-imitating-language-via-scal.tldr: A scalable inverse reinforcement learning formulation improves the performance–diversity balance of language model imitation on fixed fine-tuning datasets.

paragraphs: Lip-syncing forgeries can preserve a person's identity and lack obvious visual artifacts, making them difficult for existing deepfake detectors. The authors' preliminary experiments find that established methods often lose substantial effectiveness on these videos. Their proposed detector focuses on inconsistencies between the timing of lip movements and the accompanying audio.

The approach also uses subtle biological relationships between the lips and head regions to improve accuracy. This adds another source of evidence beyond audiovisual timing. To support evaluation and further research, the authors create AVLips, a high-quality, diverse lip-sync dataset produced using state-of-the-art lip generators.

Experiments report average detection accuracy above 95.3%, significantly outperforming the evaluated baselines. Additional tests support robustness to diverse input transformations and demonstrate performance in real-world scenarios such as WeChat video calls, with accuracy reaching 90.2%. These results indicate that temporal and biological consistency can provide useful evidence for detecting lip forgeries even when their appearance offers few obvious clues.
neurips-2024-lips-are-lying-spotting-the.tldr: A lip-forgery detector uses audiovisual timing and lip–head relationships, achieving strong reported results on generated and real-world videos.

paragraphs: Instruction tuning depends on both the quality and quantity of training examples. MAmmoTH2 explores how to obtain those examples from material already present in a pretraining web corpus. The authors harvest 10 million naturally occurring instruction examples, avoiding the need to create this dataset through costly human annotation or GPT-4 distillation.

The pipeline first retrieves relevant documents, then extracts instruction-response pairs, and finally refines those pairs using open-source language models. Fine-tuning base models on the resulting dataset produces the MAmmoTH2 family. This turns existing web content into structured training material intended to strengthen reasoning.

For MAmmoTH2-7B based on Mistral, reported performance rises from 11% to 36.7% on MATH and from 36% to 68.4% on GSM8K without training on in-domain data. Additional training on public instruction datasets produces MAmmoTH2-Plus, which achieves state-of-the-art results on several reasoning and chatbot benchmarks. The experiments demonstrate the value of extracting and refining web instructions at scale.
neurips-2024-mammoth2-scaling-instructio.tldr: MAmmoTH2 harvests 10 million web instruction examples and uses them to substantially improve language model reasoning.

paragraphs: Bi-level optimization handles learning problems in which one optimization process depends on another. Scaling these methods to large deep networks creates difficulties with memory use and gradient approximation. This paper introduces Forward Gradient Unrolling with Forward Gradient, abbreviated (FG)²U, to address those difficulties in computing the meta-gradient.

The method produces an unbiased stochastic approximation of that gradient. The authors report substantially more accurate gradient estimates than existing approaches intended for large-scale bi-level optimization, while avoiding memory and approximation issues associated with classical methods. Its design also supports parallel computation, allowing distributed systems to contribute to computational efficiency.

The paper discusses using (FG)²U alongside other methods at different training stages to form a more cost-effective two-phase procedure. It also describes implementation in common deep learning frameworks and adaptation to zeroth-order bi-level optimization. Convergence analysis and extensive experiments support the approach, with reported superior performance across diverse large-scale tasks. These contributions address both the mathematical quality of the gradient estimate and practical scaling.
neurips-2024-memory-efficient-gradient-u.tldr: (FG)²U provides unbiased stochastic meta-gradient estimates with memory-efficient, parallel computation for large-scale bi-level optimization.

paragraphs: Contrastive divergence is a method for training unnormalized models. This paper examines how accurately it can recover the parameter governing the data distribution. Its contribution is a non-asymptotic analysis, giving a finite-data perspective on an algorithm whose earlier convergence results were stated asymptotically.

For exponential-family distributions, prior work established an O(n^(-1/3)) asymptotic rate. The new analysis shows that contrastive divergence can achieve the parametric O(n^(-1/2)) rate. The faster rate means that the theoretical estimation error can decrease more quickly as the amount of data grows. The results address multiple ways of organizing data during training, including fully online processing and minibatches.

The paper also establishes near-optimality in a second sense: the algorithm's asymptotic variance is close to the Cramér–Rao lower bound. This compares its long-run statistical variability with a fundamental estimation benchmark. Together, the rate and variance results strengthen the theoretical case for contrastive divergence as an efficient estimation method, while retaining the distinction between finite-data analysis and asymptotic efficiency.
neurips-2024-near-optimality-of-contrast.tldr: New analysis shows contrastive divergence can achieve the parametric estimation rate and asymptotic variance close to a fundamental lower bound.

paragraphs: Graph representations can reveal sensitive network structure even when the original edges are not directly exposed. This paper studies similarity-based edge reconstruction attacks, or SERA, which infer connections from learned representations. Its main focus is a non-asymptotic theoretical analysis of how much graph structure these attacks can recover.

Empirical results indicate that such attacks can perfectly reconstruct sparse graphs as graph size increases. The authors also examine dense stochastic block models and show, through theory and experiments, that sparsity is a critical factor in attack effectiveness. The findings therefore connect reconstruction vulnerability to properties of the underlying graph, rather than treating attack success as uniform across graph structures.

The paper further studies representations produced with noisy aggregation, a privacy mechanism called NAG. Theory and experiments support its ability to mitigate SERA. Additional empirical analysis identifies cases where SERA is useful, and cases where it is deficient, as a tool for examining privacy–utility trade-offs. This qualifies what reconstruction attacks can reveal about representation privacy.
neurips-2024-on-provable-privacy-vulnera.tldr: The paper analyzes graph reconstruction attacks, identifies sparsity as crucial to their effectiveness, and shows mitigation through noisy aggregation.

paragraphs: The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure controls false discoveries when many statistical tests are performed together. Because this control supports applications including anomaly and out-of-distribution detection, the paper asks whether an adversary can undermine it by altering test scores. The focus is on identifying conditions under which the procedure is or is not robust.

The authors develop simple, implementable algorithms for adversarial test perturbations and evaluate them computationally. They demonstrate conditions where changing only a few scores, sometimes just one, can substantially disrupt false-discovery-rate control. They also provide non-asymptotic guarantees concerning the expected adversarial change to that rate.

The analysis recasts the procedure as a combinatorial balls-into-bins process and connects it to generalized ballot problems. These connections enable an information-theoretic derivation of finite-sample lower bounds. The resulting contribution combines explicit attacks with theoretical explanations of their effect. Its central implication is conditional: standard false-discovery control can be vulnerable to small, strategically chosen perturbations in the settings identified.
neurips-2024-on-the-adversarial-robustne.tldr: Under identified conditions, even one adversarial test-score change can substantially undermine Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery control.

paragraphs: Agencies releasing information from confidential data must balance analytical usefulness with protection against disclosure. In differential privacy, the privacy budget ε expresses this trade-off. This paper provides a framework for choosing that budget by connecting it to Bayesian probabilities of disclosure, making the choice interpretable in terms of accepted risk.

The framework distinguishes prior risk from posterior risk: the disclosure risk before the release and the risk after accounting for the released information. An agency specifies how much posterior risk it will accept at different levels of prior risk. Within the framework, that risk profile implies a unique value of ε.

This approach gives the agency a concrete basis for evaluating alternative privacy budgets. It can compare different acceptable-risk profiles and consider the resulting balance between confidentiality and analytical utility. The contribution is a decision framework linking a technical privacy parameter to explicit risk preferences. The agency still determines which risk profile is acceptable, but the framework translates that choice into the budget.
neurips-2024-prior-itizing-privacy-a-bay.tldr: A Bayesian framework translates an agency's acceptable disclosure-risk profile into a unique differential privacy budget.

paragraphs: Estimating a graph's edge density means measuring how densely its nodes are connected. This paper addresses that task while combining differential node privacy, robustness, and efficient computation. Its setting covers Erdős–Rényi random graphs and the broader class of inhomogeneous random graphs.

The algorithm combines two ingredients. First, the authors develop a sum-of-squares algorithm for robust edge-density estimation. Second, they use an existing reduction that turns robustness into privacy through sum-of-squares exponential mechanisms. This connection allows a robust estimation method to form the basis of a private algorithm, bringing the two requirements into a common construction.

The resulting method runs in polynomial time, whereas previous algorithms required either exponential time or less favorable error rates. Information-theoretic lower bounds show that its error rate is optimal up to logarithmic factors. The significance is the simultaneous achievement of computational efficiency, node privacy, robustness, and near-optimal accuracy for the stated random-graph families. The lower bounds establish that the accuracy improvement approaches a fundamental statistical limit.
neurips-2024-private-edge-density-estima.tldr: A polynomial-time algorithm estimates random-graph edge density with node privacy, robustness, and error optimal up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Convolution is a central feature-extraction operation in 3D networks, but its effectiveness can weaken under certain conditions. This paper develops an alternative based on ℓp norms and studies its suitability for point-cloud tasks. A universal approximation theorem supplies theoretical support for the expressive capacity of this convolution family.

The analysis distinguishes the consequences of different norm choices. Convolution based on the ℓ∞ norm is prone to losing features, while the ℓ2 version is essentially a linear transformation of traditional convolution. The authors identify ℓ1-based convolution as an economical and effective feature extractor, making it the focus of their practical network design.

They introduce optimization strategies tailored to ℓ1-based networks to accelerate training and improve performance, along with a convergence guarantee based on a regret argument. Experiments integrate the methods into established networks. The results show competitive performance relative to traditional convolutional networks, with lower energy consumption and instruction latency. The contribution connects the mathematical choice of feature operation with observed computational benefits.
neurips-2024-rethinking-3d-convolution-i.tldr: Norm-based 3D convolution, especially the ℓ1 form, delivers competitive experimental performance with lower energy consumption and instruction latency.

paragraphs: Second-order optimization methods use curvature information to guide updates and can converge rapidly near a solution. With noisy Hessian estimates, however, many methods require increasingly costly iterations to obtain superlinear convergence. Earlier Hessian averaging work avoided that growing cost, but could take many iterations to reach its fast local regime.

This paper proposes a stochastic Newton proximal extragradient method for strongly convex functions with access to noisy Hessian information. It extends the Hybrid Proximal Extragradient framework to combine faster global progress with rapid local convergence. The distinction matters because a strong local rate is less useful if reaching the region where it applies is slow.

The method reaches the same stated superlinear rate after roughly κ iterations, up to logarithmic factors, compared with roughly κ² for the earlier method, where κ is the condition number. It also improves the global linear convergence rate. These bounds strengthen both phases of the optimization process under the paper's strongly convex, noisy-Hessian setting.
neurips-2024-stochastic-newton-proximal-.tldr: A stochastic Newton method improves global convergence and reaches its superlinear phase in roughly κ rather than κ² iterations.

paragraphs: Most graph neural networks require a separate explanation method to make their predictions understandable. This paper introduces the Graph Neural Additive Network, or GNAN, whose design directly exposes how features and graph relationships influence predictions. It extends generalized additive models to learning on graph-structured data.

GNAN is intended to support both global explanations of model behavior and local explanations of individual predictions. Its visualizations operate at the feature and graph levels and describe the model's actual use of relationships among inputs, graph structure, and the target. That direct connection is central to the approach: the visualizations express how the model computes its answers.

The authors demonstrate intelligibility through examples across different tasks and datasets. They also report accuracy on par with black-box graph neural networks in their evaluations. The findings suggest that this architecture can combine transparent behavior with competitive predictive performance. That combination is relevant to applications where users need to understand graph-based decisions as well as obtain accurate predictions.
neurips-2024-the-intelligible-and-effect.tldr: GNAN makes graph predictions directly interpretable through an additive architecture while matching black-box GNN accuracy in reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Compact data structures can approximate the logistic-regression loss without retaining all the original data. This paper asks how much storage such approximations fundamentally require. It focuses on relative-error guarantees and a data-dependent complexity measure, μ, which already appears in storage bounds for existing coreset constructions.

When μ is bounded by a constant, the authors establish a space lower bound of roughly d/ε², up to lower-order factors. This shows that existing coresets are essentially optimal in that regime. For constant approximation error, they also prove a general lower bound of roughly dμ, up to logarithmic factors. Dependence on μ therefore reflects a broader storage requirement, rather than merely a restriction of mergeable coresets.

The paper additionally shows that μ can be computed efficiently through a linear programming formulation, refuting a previous conjecture of computational difficulty. Empirical comparisons examine this algorithm against earlier approximate methods. Together, these results clarify both the unavoidable memory cost of loss approximation and the tractability of calculating a measure that governs that cost.
neurips-2024-the-space-complexity-of-app.tldr: Storage lower bounds establish near-optimality of logistic-loss coresets in a stated regime, while linear programming makes their complexity measure efficiently computable.

paragraphs: The reversal curse occurs when a language model learns a relation in one direction but fails to recover the equivalent relation expressed in reverse. This paper investigates how training can produce that failure. It analyzes stochastic gradient descent for a bilinear model and, under specified assumptions, one-layer Transformers.

The analysis identifies asymmetry in effective model weights as the mechanism. Increasing the learned connection from token A to token B does not necessarily increase the connection from B to A. Under the studied choices of loss function and parameter optimization space, training dynamics can therefore strengthen one direction without establishing its reverse.

This perspective examines what optimization actually learns, complementing analyses concerned with what an architecture can represent. The authors explain that their analysis can also apply to other reasoning tasks, including chain-of-thought reasoning. Experiments on multilayer Transformers in different settings support the theory. The formal explanation remains tied to the analyzed models and assumptions, while the experiments investigate its relevance to deeper architectures.
neurips-2024-towards-a-theoretical-under.tldr: Training-dynamics analysis links the reversal curse to asymmetric learned connections in simplified autoregressive models, with supporting multilayer experiments.
